BREAKING: The US personal savings rate fell -0.5 percentage points in August, to 4.1%, the lowest level since November 2021.

Since January 2025, this figure has declined -1.6 percentage points.

Excluding the 2022 drop, when elevated inflation eroded purchasing power and forced American households to spend more on essentials, the savings rate is now at its lowest level since 2008.

Meanwhile, the 5-year average of this metric fell to 5.4%, the lowest in 14 years.

By comparison, before the 2020 pandemic, the average savings rate was ~6.0%.

Households are depleting their savings amid ongoing inflation.

a16z's David George on product cycles versus capital cycles, and his scorecard for the last 15 years of tech:

"AI is unique because if you throw more money at it, it can just scale up and get better. That is different than previous cycles."

"If you threw endless amounts of money at ServiceNow or Workday or Salesforce during the SaaS era, they would get all messed up... Whereas if you put $40 billion towards training these models, they get much better."

"I think about the world as product cycles and capital cycles... In 2021, we were at like a 1 out of 10. We didn't realize it at the time. That was late SaaS, late cloud, post-mobile phone growth... There was no room for something new."

"In 2010 it was like an 8 out of 10. Right now product cycle is like a 9 or 10."

"Your ideal would be a 10 on product cycle and a 10 on capital cycle, meaning valuations are really low. They almost never coincide."

"Like 2023, early days of when AI started working... capital cycle was like a 7... Right now we're probably at a 6. It's okay, but not great."

"But the thing that drives our business over 10 years, whether it's venture or growth, is the product cycles. And that's like a 9 or 10 right now."

@DavidGeorge83 w/ @jaltma

US equity ETFs attracted +$3.3 billion in inflows on average per day in September, the lowest reading since March.

This also marks the 3rd consecutive monthly decline.

By comparison, these funds attracted a record +$7.0 billion in inflows on average per day in June.

September’s figure is now lower than the daily average of +$3.7 billion seen in 2025.

However, this is still more than double the levels seen in 2022 and 2023.

Buyers are taking a breather.

AI is all that matters for markets right now.

AI infrastructure companies now account for 40% of the S&P 500’s market capitalization.

At the same time, just 3 chipmaker firms represent 28% of the MSCI Emerging Markets Index.

AI-related companies also account for 49% of investment-grade bond issuance so far in 2026.

The concentration is even more extreme in private markets, with AI capturing 87% of venture capital funding year-to-date.

By comparison, in 1999, during the Dot-Com bubble, less than 40% of venture capital funding was related to internet companies.

AI has become the market.

Investors have rarely been this bullish on tech.

Long speculative positioning in Nasdaq futures is up to nearly 50% of open interest, its highest since 2017.

This covers hedge funds, CTAs, and other institutional investors trading Nasdaq futures.

In other words, the net long Nasdaq futures position of these investors equals ~50% of all currently open Nasdaq futures contracts.

This marks a sharp reversal from a net short position as a % of open interest just a few weeks ago.

By comparison, Nasdaq net long positioning was below 25% of open interest for most of 2021-2025.

Meanwhile, net short positioning in Russell 2000 futures is down to -30% of open interest, its most bearish level since late 2025.

Investors are becoming extremely bullish on tech.

For the third straight month, a "Too Hot" number is the biggest risk. It pushes yields higher and turns one more rate hike in 2026 into two.

Economic data has run hot lately. A blowout jobs number on top of that tells the Fed the labor market can take more hikes.

Jobs Report Preview: One Rate Hike or Two?

Good news for the economy is bad news for this market right now, because every hot labor report hands the Fed another reason to keep hiking 🧵

Worse, it proves inflation is about more than oil.

Oil will fall eventually. It's only a matter of time. But if wages are doing some of the work, the Fed may not soften when oil drops, and markets have been betting that it will.

Right now the Fed doesn't believe a tight labor market is feeding inflation.

If the labor market heats up further, the argument that rising wages push prices higher starts to carry real weight. That makes the Fed structurally more hawkish.

Don't ignore a weak report either. A slowdown is the most serious threat to this bull market.

But claims, ADP and JOLTS all look fine, and retail sales and flash PMIs are accelerating. One bad number is an outlier, and markets will discount it, at least at first.

Bottom line: tomorrow's report matters for one reason: it's a hit to Fed hike expectations.

The more Goldilocks the number, meaning positive job adds but only modestly so, the better for markets. That signals solid growth with potentially fewer hikes.

tweets.text: Earnings strength is the greatest insulation from growing macro risk .. think of EPS growth as the "R" measure.. Tech must be something close to a R-50?! Over the past 4m (6/1), the SPX is up 87bp. There has been winners and losers, if you look at the industry list you can see the impact of rates going from 4.45 to >5%, as most industries with loses are more rate-sensitive like Autos, Durables, Utilities and Telco. While the big winners are Pharma and Energy. Energy is the only group that has a persistent positive correlation to interest rates across history. Tech has continued to gain, carrying the S&P 500 cap-weighed index. It looks worse as you go down cap, the losses are larger and broader.

Well, folks, it's that time of the cycle. When the tension between debt and the liquidity to support it, starts sending signals to the markets. In simple terms, debt has risen faster than liquidity since 2021 and this means tension in the system previously hidden starts bubbling to the surface.
It shows up in many forms - sometimes it's the financial plumbing seizing up (2019, Q42025), bank failures, sovereign crises, etc. Most visibly, it shows up in the dollar, the MOVE index, long-bond yields, and credit. All are speaking up right now.  
Historically, this doesn't bode well for risk assets like equities and liquidity-sensitive assets like $BTC. The usual playbook suggests risk sells off, and the central planners rush in after a flush with new 'temporary' measures. These cycles are around 5 years and we are due. Interestingly, Bitcoin had a deeper reset sooner than I anticipated (I thought it would happen around now), which makes this round so interesting. Without the embedded leverage and overstretched positioning typically associated with this point in the cycle, I think Bitcoin will surprise if there is a risk-off period.
